opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one of the big shifts going from AlphaFold 2 to AlphaFold 3 was that we wanted to move beyond just proteins. We wanted to model essentially everything you find in the Protein Data Bank: proteins, but also DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, ions, chemical modifications, all interacting together. Once you open the door that wide, the way you represent structure has to change.

AlphaFold 2 had a structure module that was quite specialized for proteins. It reasoned about residues as rigid frames with torsion angles, a lot of carefully engineered, protein-specific geometry. That worked beautifully for proteins, but it doesn't generalize nicely to an arbitrary small molecule, where you don't have that same residue-based chemistry.

Diffusion let us step back and operate directly on raw atom coordinates. The model starts from noise and iteratively denoises toward a plausible structure, and it doesn't need to know ahead of time whether an atom belongs to a protein, a nucleic acid, or a drug-like ligand. The same machinery applies to all of them. That simplicity was a big part of the appeal. We could remove a lot of the bespoke components and let the network learn the chemistry from the data.

There are a couple of other nice properties too. Diffusion works across multiple scales. At high noise levels the model learns the large-scale arrangement, how different chains and molecules pack together. At low noise levels it focuses on fine local detail like bond geometry and stereochemistry. You get both the global and the local picture in one framework.

It's also a generative model, so you get a distribution of structures rather than a single regression output. That matters because a lot of biology is ambiguous or flexible, and a generative approach handles it more gracefully than averaging everything into one blurry answer.

It wasn't free, though. Generative models can hallucinate, especially in disordered regions, where they might invent structure that isn't really there. We had to address that, partly by training on AlphaFold 2 predictions, which tend to show disordered regions as extended loops, so the model learned that behavior instead of making things up. But overall, diffusion was what made it practical to have one general model that handles all these molecule types together, and that's really the core of what AlphaFold 3 is.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is what the problem actually looked like once you moved beyond proteins. With AlphaFold 2, the whole architecture was built around the protein-specific picture of the world. You have residues, you have a frame per residue, and a lot of the structure module was really about rotating and translating those rigid frames and then filling in the side-chain atoms with torsion angles. That worked beautifully for proteins, but the moment you want to handle DNA, RNA, small-molecule ligands, ions, covalent modifications, all of that, the notion of a "residue frame" starts to break down. A ligand doesn't have a backbone. An ion is a single atom. So you'd end up writing special cases for every molecule type, and that's just not a scalable way to build a general model.

What diffusion gave us was a way to throw all of that away and work directly on raw atom coordinates. Every entity in the system is just a cloud of atoms in 3D space, and the model's job is to take a noisy version of those coordinates and denoise it. It doesn't need to know a priori whether an atom belongs to a protein or a nucleotide or a drug molecule in terms of how it's represented geometrically. That uniformity was the big win. One generative process for everything.

The second thing, which I think is a bit more subtle, is that diffusion naturally handles the multi-scale nature of the problem. At high noise levels, the model is essentially reasoning about the coarse global arrangement, where do the chains go relative to each other, where does the ligand sit in the pocket. And as the noise comes down, it's refining local geometry, bond lengths, the precise orientation of a side chain against an aromatic ring. You get that hierarchy for free from the noise schedule rather than having to engineer it.

And then there's the question of what you do with uncertainty. Regression-style models, which is roughly what the AlphaFold 2 structure module was, tend to average over possibilities when they're unsure, and you get these smeared, physically implausible outputs. A diffusion model is generative, so it commits to a sample. That meant we could drop a lot of the hand-built stereochemical losses and penalties that had been needed to keep the geometry sensible, because the model was learning the distribution of real structures and producing samples that look like real structures. It also opens the door to sampling multiple times and getting a sense of which parts of the complex are confidently placed and which aren't.

I'll be honest, it wasn't obvious going in that it would work this well. There were real concerns about hallucination, the model producing something that looks confident and plausible in a region where it actually has no idea. We had to do things like cross-distillation training to deal with that. But once it clicked, the generality was the payoff. The same model handling a protein-protein interface, a protein-DNA interaction, and a small molecule in a binding site, with one architecture and one training objective.

astra-6.text:
The key thing is that diffusion gives you a very general way to generate three-dimensional structures. When you move beyond proteins to complexes that include DNA, RNA, small molecules, and ions, you want a representation that works across all of those different types of molecules. At the level of atomic coordinates, they can all be treated within the same framework.

You start with noisy coordinates, and the model learns to progressively remove that noise, conditioned on the molecules involved and the information it has extracted about their interactions. That lets you model the whole complex jointly, so the shape of a ligand and the shape of its binding pocket can be predicted together.

It’s also a natural way to represent the fact that there can be multiple plausible structures. Rather than having to average those possibilities into a single prediction, you can sample distinct, coherent arrangements. So it gives you both a flexible representation across molecule types and a powerful way to capture the geometry of their interactions.

sol-6.1.text:
What was really attractive about diffusion was that we could model all these different molecules in a very general way: as atoms in three-dimensional space. Whether you’re dealing with a protein, DNA, RNA, or a small molecule, ultimately you need to predict where those atoms go and how they interact.

With AlphaFold 2, we had built a lot of protein-specific knowledge into the architecture. That was incredibly effective for proteins, but harder to extend to all these other molecule types. Diffusion gave us a much more general framework. You start with noisy atomic coordinates and iteratively refine them, conditioned on the molecular inputs, into a coherent structure.

And that’s particularly useful because the interactions are coupled. You don’t just want to predict a protein and then separately fit a ligand into it; you want to model the whole complex together, so that the different molecules can influence one another’s predicted structure.
